raw:
When Ashworth pauses over his folder, you ask how a student in the human seat is meant to learn its practical duties.

The Chancellor’s gaze settles on you without surprise.

“By stages, Mr. Garvey—and first by being precise about what you presently are.” He rests a hand on the black folder. “The Council has verified your inheritance. It has not yet filled its vacant human seat. You have no vote, no authority to bind the human signatory to an agreement, and no Council privilege beyond what is granted to every Conclave student.”

Aldric’s papers stop rustling. Across the table, Ashara sits a little straighter.

“That does not mean we leave you with a primer and good wishes,” Ashworth continues. “The first year’s work is procedure, case law, drafting, negotiation exercises, and committee briefs. You will do all of it beside your peers. Professor Stone will serve as your academic adviser for documented human Covenant history and institutional precedent.”

At Stone’s name, the room gives nothing away; the professor is not present.

“Beginning next month, you will also spend two afternoons each month with the Academy’s Council Liaison Office. You will observe how agendas are circulated, how delegations amend proposals before they reach a chamber, and how commissions keep records. In the winter term, you will undertake the same supervised placement expected of every Conclave student—adapted, in your case, because there is no functioning human delegation to receive you.”

Rashid’s thumb traces once along the edge of his papers.

“So he begins learning the work after the families of everyone else here have spent years teaching it.”

Ashworth’s expression hardens slightly. “Yes. The Council’s failure to maintain a human succession does not become less serious because it is inconvenient to say aloud.”

Ashara glances from Rashid to you, then back to the Chancellor. “At least the work can be judged.”

“It can,” Ashworth says. “And it will be.”

Caelindra turns her pen between her fingers. “Committee briefs are not governance.”

“No,” says Ashworth. “They are how one learns where governance actually occurs.”

He opens the folder again. A server from Garvey House moves around the table, laying a thin packet before each student. Yours bears your name beneath the Academy seal. Inside, one page lists the ordinary Conclave timetable; another is headed *Human Student Programme* and gives Professor Stone’s office hours, the Liaison Office rotation, and a date for a meeting with the Academy registrar.

Ashworth lets the papers settle before moving on to the morning’s introductions.
